native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The Black advantage (Black-minus-non-Black differential) in college-degree-level attainment is negatively related to family socioeconomic status: it is near zero at low parental SES (>=14yrs: 2.4% vs 2.7%; >=13yrs: 5.7% vs 4.4% - slightly positive) and declines monotonically to a large deficit at high parental SES (>=14yrs: 7.3% vs 13.6%, about 5-7pp; >=13yrs: 16.4% vs 24.2%, about 8pp). The pattern holds across >=13/>=14/>=15 thresholds and the age>=19 subsample (not an age-censoring artifact), but reverses/flattens under income- or wealth-based SES, so it is specific to exogenous background (parental-education) SES. Literal BA (grade>=16) is too sparse (0.3%) to analyze in this single 1979 snapshot.
native_result.WorkflowB: Cleaned Highest grade completed 1979 (dropped invalid grade 95, n=2; missing n=152) into thresholds >=13/>=14/>=15/>=16. Built SES measures (parental-education composite with one-parent fallback; family income 1979; family net wealth 1996) as population terciles Low/Mid/High. Complete-case primary sample n=12,098; per-cell N reported (BLACK/HISP/NBNH: Low 1204/1106/1712, Mid 309/1005/2717, High 372/816/2857). Computed race-by-SES attainment rates plus Black-minus-pooled-nonBlack and Black-minus-NBNH advantages (pp). Fitted age-and-sex-controlled logistic regressions testing Black x SES interactions (Low-vs-High contrast and 0/1/2 linear trend). Sensitivities: age>=19 subsample (de-censoring), alternative SES measures (income79, wealth96), and parental-ed mean-imputation. All in analysis_main.py; results_summary.csv saved.

sub_hypo.text: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower socioeconomic status (SES) levels, with a coefficient of 0.7606 for the interaction between SES and being Black.
sub_hypo.context: Students in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY79), with emphasis on lower SES levels.
variables: BA degree completion rate (column not specified)
sub_hypo.relations: SES moderates the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students: the advantage is more pronounced at lower SES levels. The interaction between SES and being Black has a coefficient of 0.7606.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606

sub_hypo.text: The Black-minus-non-Black differential in college-degree-level attainment declines monotonically as parental-education SES increases, from approximately zero at low SES to a substantial deficit at high SES.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 participants in the single 1979 educational-attainment snapshot; complete-case primary sample n=12,098, excluding invalid grade 95 and missing grades. Parental-education SES uses a composite with one-parent fallback, divided into population Low/Mid/High terciles.
variables: Highest grade completed by respondent's mother, 1979
Highest grade completed by respondent's father, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: Negative Black-by-parental-SES interaction, assessed with age-and-sex-controlled logistic regressions using Low-versus-High contrasts and a 0/1/2 linear trend. At grade >=14, Black versus non-Black attainment is 2.4% versus 2.7% at low SES and 7.3% versus 13.6% at high SES; at grade >=13, it is 5.7% versus 4.4% at low SES and 16.4% versus 24.2% at high SES. Differentials are calculated against pooled non-Black respondents and non-Black non-Hispanic respondents.

sub_hypo.text: The negative relationship between parental-education SES and the Black attainment advantage holds across grade >=13, >=14, and >=15 thresholds and among respondents aged at least 19, rather than being an age-censoring artifact.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 educational attainment in 1979, evaluated across alternative attainment thresholds and in the age >=19 subsample; parental education is grouped into population SES terciles.
variables: Highest grade completed by respondent's mother, 1979
Highest grade completed by respondent's father, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: The declining Black-minus-non-Black attainment differential across parental-education SES persists across the three thresholds and after restricting age to >=19; regressions control for age and sex.

sub_hypo.text: The declining Black attainment advantage with increasing SES reverses or flattens when SES is measured by family income or wealth, making the negative pattern specific to parental-education background SES.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 attainment measured in 1979; sensitivity analyses replace parental-education SES with 1979 family income or 1996 family net wealth, each divided into population Low/Mid/High terciles.

sub_hypo.relations: The negative association between SES and the Black-minus-non-Black attainment differential under parental-education SES becomes flat or reverses under income- or wealth-based SES.
